To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the response distributions for orientation discrimination are not normally distributed, that the shape of these response distributions changes as a function of feature and spatial probabilities, and that these changes are consistent with changes in the variances and covariances of the component tuning curves of orientation-tuned cells.

(a) the response distributions for the orientation of a visual grating were changed when the probability of the conjunction of orientation and location was increased and (b) the change in the response distributions could be explained by changes in the variances and covariances of the component tuning curves that comprise a population of orientation-tuned cells.
(i) feature-based attention biases the processing of sensory features and (ii) the shape of response distributions can be altered by changing the probability of conjunctions of features.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the brain represents and processes information about the world.
the role of probability in visual perception and attention.
the mechanisms of attention and how they affect perception.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
attention changes the shape of the distribution of responses to stimuli.
attention changes the shape of the distribution of responses to a sensory event.
feature-based attention does not operate independently of spatial attention.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the probability of the conjunction of features and locations can be used to bias the response distribution.
feature-based attention is not a spatially invariant process but instead a mechanism that is sensitive to the probability of conjunctions of features.
attention is not a mechanism for enhancing perceptual processing but for prioritizing some stimuli over others.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distribution of responses to a set of stimuli can change dramatically with the introduction of attention.
the effects of feature-based attention are more complicated than is often assumed.

the effects of spatial attention on the shape of the orientation discrimination function are not consistent with a model that assumes that attention is a spatially invariant process that biases the processing of sensory features.
